o: We maintain a rectangle and support two operations: paint a subrectangle with a single value, and read a single cell. With at most 500 operations and a grid of at most 100x100, even the naive approach of rewriting every cell on each update costs at most 500 * 10,000 = 5,000,000 cell writes, which is trivially fast. In Example 1, updating (0,0)-(3,2) to 5 overwrites everything, then updating row 3 to 10 only changes that row; getValue simply reads the current matrix. The tiny constraints mean we should favor simplicity: either mutate the grid directly, or record updates lazily and scan them backwards on reads.
k: With ≤500 operations on a ≤100×100 grid, brute-force updates are at most ~5M writes — well within limits.
A lazy approach stores each update as a tuple and answers getValue by scanning updates in reverse order, returning the first one covering the cell.
Lazy updates make getValue O(#updates) but updateSubrectangle O(1), which is ideal if updates vastly outnumber reads.

a.i: Keep the matrix as-is. On updateSubrectangle, loop over every cell in the given range and overwrite it with newValue. On getValue, just return the stored value. This is the most intuitive design and easily fits the constraints since the total work is bounded by 500 × 100 × 100.
s: Store the input matrix in the constructor.
updateSubrectangle: for r from row1..row2, for c from col1..col2, set matrix[r][c] = newValue.
a.t: O(rows × cols) per update in the worst case, O(1) per getValue; with ≤500 ops and 100×100 grid, total work is ~5M operations.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the input matrix.

a.i: Instead of touching the grid on every update, append the update parameters to a history list. To answer getValue(row, col), scan the history backwards and return the first update whose rectangle contains (row, col); if none does, fall back to the original matrix value. Later updates correctly override earlier ones because of the reverse scan, and each update becomes O(1).
s: Store the original matrix plus an empty list of updates [row1, col1, row2, col2, newValue].
updateSubrectangle: append the five parameters to the updates list.
getValue: iterate updates from newest to oldest; if row1 <= row <= row2 and col1 <= col <= col2, return its newValue.
If no update covers the cell, return the original matrix value.
a.t: O(1) per updateSubrectangle; O(U) per getValue where U is the number of updates so far (≤500 here).
a.sp: O(U) extra space for the update log, O(1) otherwise.

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1 — it is simple, obviously correct, and comfortably fits the constraints; mention Approach 2 as an optimization when updates are frequent and reads are rare (or when the grid were huge). Common pitfalls: off-by-one errors on inclusive bounds (use `<=` for row2/col2), forgetting the fallback to the original matrix in the lazy approach, and mutating the caller's matrix in Java/C++ (fine here, but note it). Edge cases: single-cell rectangles, full-grid updates, and repeated overlapping updates — both approaches handle these naturally. Likely follow-ups: what if there are millions of operations? Then use a 2D segment tree or a KD-tree/interval structure for O(log² n) point queries and range assignment; also discuss making getValue O(log U) with an interval tree over the update log.
